thread.title: Shakespeare is the Key to Understanding Trump
thread.title_full: Shakespeare is the Key to Understanding Trump

author: James Alexander
title: Shakespeare is the Key to Understanding Trump
text:
We read novels. We are made to read poetry. We hardly ever read plays. And it is something of an acquired art to read plays. Every time I have ventured into reading plays I have had to adjust my eye, and sensibility: it takes some time. And plays are a great art form. Theatre. Drama. Comedy. Tragedy. The great tradition from Aeschylus, via Sophocles and Euripides, through the Romans like Terence and Seneca and through Mystery plays to the revived drama of, eminently, Shakespeare, Marlow and Jonson and Calderon and Lope de Vega, and then everyone: Corneille, Racine, Dryden, Sheridan, even Tennyson, and then Ibsen, Shaw, Yeats, Eliot, Brecht and so on: with a last burst of enthusiasm in the 1950s, with Osborne, Arden, Bond, running through to the 1970s with Hare, Brenton et al. : who more or less murdered the drama in agitprop, though it was also eaten away by film and television.
A century ago the consensus was that the two greatest playwrights in English were Shakespeare (1550-1604) and Shaw (1856-1950). We would dispute this now: Shaw’s flame is down. I think it will revive. Disagree? Try You Never Can Tell or The Man of Destiny or The Doctor’s Dilemma or Getting Married or, hell’s bells, even Shakes Versus Shav , a very late play in which Shaw put himself and Shakespeare on the stage at the same time to knock each other about. Shaw put himself in the same category as Shakespeare: not only admiring him, but asking, famously, in the 1890s, whether he, Shaw, was ‘Better than Shakespear?’, and also refinishing Cymbeline , which he thought was a terrible clockwork plot of Shakespeare’s making. Shakespeare had written Julius Caesar and Antony and Cleopatra : so Shaw gave us Caesar and Cleopatra . The hero of Man and Superman was his Hamlet, overcoming confusion and therefore of interest to his Ophelia. Etc.
I want to take these two men to be archetypes for two visions of politics.
Shakespeare is medieval politics.
Shaw is modern politics.
I was planning to write something about this, but then I heard the great David Starkey say emphatically that Trump is Henry VIII.
Voila ! For that is the point.
Starkey is at least two things. He is a Tudor historian – he knows about the Shakespearian era. And he is a historian of the court. If one ever listens to Starkey one has to listen to talk about an old historian called G.R. Elton, his ‘mentor’. A thousand years ago, in the 1960s, Elton wanted to be Starkey’s ‘line manager’, but Starkey would not have it. This is because Elton, a vast figure from the 1950s onwards, though not much known now, was the historian of The System: of bureaucracy, of administration, of efficiency, of impersonality, of, above all, Thomas Cromwell. Elton argued that England became a Utilitarian Calculus of Administrative Impersonal Efficiency in the 1530s. Starkey said, ‘Rubbish!’, slipped the leash, and became the antitype of Elton. He made himself a historian of the Court.
Court is unlike Council or Secretaryship. Court is flamboyant. It is the Earl of Oxford and Sir Philip Sidney having a row at a tennis court, and being told off by the Queen. It is a matter of masque and murder. It is, in a word, Shakespeare. It is noble, also ignoble, and monarchical.
So when Starkey says that Trump is Henry VIII he means: Trump is a monarch, sees himself as a monarch, and a Trump politics is a court politics: and, what is more, an outward facing court politics: with a certain amount of transparency. We see the conflict. It is not hidden behind the closed doors and rushing up and down the corridors of power. It is made a matter of public concern: pomp and ceremony and crisis.
This is absolutely right. It explains, by the way, why almost all the newspapers have Trump’s regime absolutely wrong. The Guardian , even the Spectator , complain about Trump as if he is not cricket. But what they mean, if they were capable of recognising it, is that Trump is not system-politics, is not deep-state politics, is not council politics. Trump is court politics. Anyone who wants to understand Trump has to think of Elizabeth I with her lead-white visage and those astonishing paintings like the Rainbow painting: or Henry VIII with his colossal shoulders and codpiece: or, if one prefers, a three-headed Charles I by Van Dyke, or Charles I on a horse, also by Van Dyke. It is no good thinking of Rylance’s Cromwell or Disraeli’s Queen Victoria or our own Elizabeth II: good, unaesthetic Lilibet. Lilibet lived in the era of Shaw. Bess lived in the era of Shakespeare.
This is why we need Shakespeare.
What was all that study of Shakespeare at school about, if not enabling us to understand Trump?
If we return to Shaw. Shakespeare was a poet and playwright. Shaw was a playwright, critic and politician of sorts. He thought himself inferior to Shakespeare as a word musician. But he thought himself superior to Shakespeare in having ideas in his head. Whereas Shakespeare’s plays were all about individual souls confusedly entertaining temptation, Shaw’s plays were about individual souls caught in a matrix. In Shakespeare there was no escape from tragedy. In Shaw there was the possibility of a comedic future in which we could escape, like Bunyan’s Pilgrim, from tragedy, doom, disaster and the slough of despond. The escape was, as we know, Socialist. Well! But Shaw took politics to be a matter of institution, constitution, party, policy, programme: and he said, “There is nothing of this in Shakespeare.”
We may like Shakespeare and not Shaw, but we must face the fact that in the 20th century our politics was Shavian, not Shakespearian. Shaw himself was a Shakespearian, or Dickensian character: free, eccentric, like Falstaff without the sack. But his suggested escape from the world was everything he was not: it was uniform, safe, secure, and a bit dull. A sort of infinite projection of a cross between the NHS and the National Theatre.
Now, by and large, our political writers, and the journalists we still read, even now, seem to have a view of politics that is Shavian and dull. We expect politicians to be hypocrites of the system. And so no one understands Trump. He is, to our minds, a short-circuit, a stroke, a Deus ex machina , an Absolutely Unthinkable. Even in the Spectator there seems to be a concerted effort to disapprove of Trump as an affront to politics. But why? Because we do not understand that politics is, politics was and politics always will be, as much about Court as it is about Council, and, at root, that the Court is more fundamental than the Council. Trump is the truth of the system. But believers in the system deny it.
And that is our condition. We have had a politics, since the Second World War, of the political denial of politics. Our politics has things in it that Shakespeare never dreamed of, but the Shavian politics did not eliminate the Shakespearian politics. It just overlaid it: and the Falstaffian, Coriolanian, Macbethian elements will out.
James Alexander is a Professor in the Department of Political Science at Bilkent University in Turkey.
